item.title: Johann Weyer (1515–1588): Medical Demonology and the Critique of Witchcraft Prosecution
item.description:
Life and Medical Authority

Johann Weyer (1515–1588), Dutch physician and demonologist, became one of the most influential early modern critics of witchcraft persecution through his De Praestigiis Daemonum (On the Illusions of Demons, 1563). Though Weyer accepted the reality of demons, he argued that most witchcraft accusations involved either demon-possessed persons (needing medical/spiritual treatment, not execution) or deluded people (victims of disease, not criminals).

Born in Grave, trained in medicine at Paris and Orleans, Weyer practiced as a physician and served as court physician to the Duke of Cleves. His medical background gave him authority in claiming that alleged witches were actually mentally or physically ill persons requiring treatment rather than punishment.

item.title: Reginald Scot (1538–1599): Witchcraft Skepticism and the Critique of Magical Claims
item.description:
Life and Intellectual Mission

Reginald Scot (1538–1599), English country gentleman and writer, became one of the most important early modern critics of witchcraft panic through his Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584). Published during the height of English witchcraft prosecutions, Scot’s work argued that alleged witches possessed no real magical powers and that witchcraft accusations were based on delusion, fraud, or natural causes.

Though Scot had no formal academic training, his practical observation and logical argumentation made his work influential among educated readers. His Discoverie provided rational skepticism grounded in natural philosophy rather than mere denial of witchcraft’s possibility.
